title: Imperatives and classroom language: cumulative review
objectives: Give positive and negative classroom instructions.
Make courteous requests using please or could.
Review earlier verb forms and pronouns in classroom contexts.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: An imperative is a verb form used to give an instruction, make a request or give advice. In a classroom, a teacher might say ‘Open your books’ or ‘Listen carefully’. The person listening is usually understood, so we do not normally write or say the subject you. The context and tone tell us whether the sentence sounds like an instruction, a request or advice.

This unit also reviews language from earlier lessons. You will use present simple forms for routines, present continuous forms for actions now, pronouns to refer to people, and can or could for requests. These forms can all be useful when people work together in a classroom.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: For a positive imperative, start with the base form of the verb: ‘Read the question’, ‘Write your name’ or ‘Be quiet’. Use the same form for one listener and for several listeners. You can add please to make a request more polite: ‘Please sit down’ or ‘Sit down, please’. A polite tone also matters.

For a negative imperative, put do not or don’t before the base form: ‘Don’t talk during the recording’ and ‘Please don’t open the window’. Use don’t be with the verb be: ‘Don’t be late’. Do not add -s to the verb. A written imperative often ends with a full stop; an exclamation mark can show a stronger tone.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Instructions can have more than one step: ‘Read the text and answer the questions’. In class, you may also hear ‘Work in pairs’, ‘Look at the board’, ‘Check your answers’ and ‘Ask your partner’. These instructions use ordinary verbs in the base form. A partner is a person you work with.

There are other polite ways to ask someone to act. ‘Could you repeat that, please?’ is a question that makes a request; ‘Please repeat that’ is an imperative request. Both can be polite. When you need help, ‘Can you help me?’ uses the modal can and the object pronoun me.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not use an -ing form by itself for the ordinary imperative: say ‘Open your book’, not ‘Opening your book’. Do not put not after the main verb to make a negative: say ‘Don’t write’, not ‘Write not’. In a question with could, the pattern is different: ‘Could you repeat that?’ includes a subject.

An imperative can be friendly or firm. ‘Sit down’ is not automatically rude, but a direct instruction can sound abrupt in some situations. Please, the relationship between the speakers and the tone all affect the message. This review combines classroom language with grammar from earlier units.

examples.sentence: Open your books at page ten.
examples.note: Open is the base form in an instruction.
Please makes the instruction more courteous.

examples.sentence: Don’t use your phone during the test.

examples.note: Use don’t before the base form be.
Could you introduces a polite question used as a request.

examples.sentence: Work in pairs and check your answers.
examples.note: Two base verbs give two instructions.
Her is an object pronoun after to.

common_errors.reason: Use the base form open in an imperative.
Use don’t before the base verb for a negative imperative.
Use the base form be after don’t.

summary: Use the base form of a verb to give an instruction or request.
Use don’t or do not before the base form for a negative instruction.
Please, could and a suitable tone can make a request more courteous.
